5500               	;
5501               	; 	' ======================================================================
5502               	; 	' DRAWING THE STORE -- four blits, once per screen crossing
5503               	; 	' ======================================================================
5504               	; 	' This is the whole cost of the flip, and it is paid on a discrete event
5505               	; 	' rather than every frame. RallyX's pan repaints 576 chars every time the
5506               	; 	' camera moves one cell; this repaints 640 about once every two seconds
5507               	; 	' of running.
5508               	; 	' SPRITES OFF BEFORE THE BLIT, NOT AFTER IT. This routine WAITs between
5509               	; 	' bands -- one band a frame, because a burst of VDP writes past a few
5510               	; 	' dozen in one frame is silently dropped -- so painting the new screen
5511               	; 	' takes several frames, and for all of them the OLD screen's actors and
5512               	; 	' obstacles were still sitting on top of it. Following Harry through a
5513               	; 	' seam showed him and every cart from the floor he had just left,
5514               	; 	' standing on a shop that was assembling itself underneath them.
5515               	; 	'
5516               	; 	' They are put back by the normal draw on the same pass, so the crossing
5517               	; 	' reads as a cut rather than as a dissolve with ghosts in it.
5518               	; 	' EACH BAND IS FINISHED BEFORE THE FRAME IT IS DRAWN IN ENDS, and the
5519               	; 	' bands go TOP DOWN. Both halves of that matter.
5520               	; 	'
5521               	; 	' The blit paints the template -- shelves, pillars and all -- and the
5522               	; 	' radios and prizes then take out the fixtures they stand in. Those two
5523               	; 	' used to be four frames apart: all four bands blitted with a WAIT
5524               	; 	' between them, and only afterwards the clearing. So every screen change
5525               	; 	' showed its counters and beams for several frames and then erased them,
5526               	; 	' which reads as the shop flickering rather than as it being drawn.
5527               	; 	'
5528               	; 	' TOP DOWN because a band's beam tops are stamped into the SLAB ROW OF
5529               	; 	' THE BAND ABOVE. Going bottom-up, band 1's blit would paint over the
5530               	; 	' beam tops band 0 had just put there. Going top-down the band above is
5531               	; 	' always already drawn, so everything a band needs -- its own cells and
5532               	; 	' the row it borrows overhead -- is final by the time its WAIT arrives.
5533               	; 	'
5534               	; 	' `3 - dq` rather than `FOR dlv = 3 TO 0 STEP -1`: dlv is an unsigned
5535               	; 	' byte, so counting down past zero wraps to 255 and the loop never ends
5536               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A).
5537               	; draw_screen:
5538               cvb_DRAW_SCREEN

5683               	;
5684               	; 	' A SUPPORT BEAM HAS TO REACH THE FLOOR IT HOLDS UP, AND THAT FLOOR IS
5685               	; 	' NOT IN ITS OWN BAND. A beam fills its band's four air rows, so its top
5686               	; 	' pixel sits under the slab row of the band ABOVE -- and a slab row is
5687               	; 	' five pixels of bar over three of green (see SLAB), so the beam stopped
5688               	; 	' three pixels short of the bar on every storey. It read as a beam that
5689               	; 	' misses the floor, which is exactly what it was.
5690               	; 	'
5691               	; 	' It cannot be drawn into either template. The beam belongs to the band
5692               	; 	' below and the row belongs to the band above, and the two templates are
5693               	; 	' chosen independently per screen, so no template knows both. So the
5694               	; 	' band blits go down first and the tops are stamped afterwards, from a
5695               	; 	' per-template column table -- the same shape as the escalator's head cap.
5696               	; 	'
5697               	; 	' Bands 0 and 1 only. Band 2's top row is the ROOF DECK, which is grey
5698               	; 	' over grey with no green to bridge, and the roof itself has no band
5699               	; 	' above it at all.
5700               	; 	' BANDS 0 TO 2 -- ALL THREE SHOPPING FLOORS. It used to stop at 1,
5701               	; 	' because band 2's ceiling is the ROOF DECK and the deck had no green
5702               	; 	' under it: a beam there already ran straight into grey and needed
5703               	; 	' nothing. Giving the roof its three green rows (so the lift shaft stops
5704               	; 	' under it, like every other floor) took that away, and the top floor's
5705               	; 	' beams started falling three pixels short.
5706               	; 	'
5707               	; 	' So the roof gets its own version of the stamp. A beam HOLDS THE ROOF
5708               	; 	' UP and must reach it; the shaft merely stops beneath it.

6494               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
6495               	; 			'
6496               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
6497               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
6498               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
6499               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
6500               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
6501               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes
6502               	; 			' the same approach at the same speed could not be jumped
6503               	; 			' at all. That is not difficulty, it is a coin toss.
6504               	; 			'
6505               	; 			' So the phase is worked BACKWARDS from the meeting. He
6506               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in
6507               	; 			' (gap / 6) passes; the phase advances one a pass and wraps
6508               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
6509               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.
6510               	; 			'
6511               	; 			' The gap is the same either way round: he enters at one
6512               	; 			' wall and the ball starts `stag` in from the other, so it
6513               	; 			' is 232 - stag whichever direction the floor runs.
6514               	; 			'
6515               	; 			' It stays forgiving rather than exact. The arc is flat near
6516               	; 			' the bottom, so anything within eight passes either side is
6517               	; 			' still under the jump; and it only holds for an unbroken
6518               	; 			' run, which is the case the player is entitled to read off
6519               	; 			' the screen. Duck, stop or take a hit and everything after
6520               	; 			' is out of step again -- which is the game.
6521               	; 			' obp is a BALL-only field: upd_obst reads it under an
6522               	; 			' IF uk = OB_BALL and nothing else touches it, and every

6937               	; 		' answer from the template and the pillar table instead of
6938               	; 		' reading the PPU, and neither lookup can be done without the
6939               	; 		' band. It is set here rather than passed, because CVBasic has
6940               	; 		' no parameters -- and it must be set at EVERY caller of
6941               	; 		' wall_clear, beam_clear or wipe_shelf, which is this routine
6942               	; 		' and radio_band.

7465               	; 		' HE IS STANDING ON A STEP, so he moves at the STEP's rate: 2 px
7466               	; 		' across and 1 up PER PASS -- the staircase's own slope, and exactly
7467               	; 		' what one phase of esc_tick moves the pattern by.
7468               	; 		'
7469               	; 		' NOT `fdv`, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT. Everything else in this loop
7470               	; 		' is paced by the frame delta, and pacing him that way too made him
7471               	; 		' outrun the steps the moment a pass cost more than one frame: his
7472               	; 		' feet started planted on a tread and ended floating above it.
7473               	; 		' Pacing the ANIMATION by fdv instead is worse -- four phases cannot
7474               	; 		' be stepped by 2 or 3 without aliasing, and the staircase runs
7475               	; 		' backwards (see esc_tick). The only arrangement that cannot drift
7476               	; 		' is the one where both are driven by the same fixed step, so the
7477               	; 		' rider is clocked by the pass, like the steps he is standing on.
7478               	; 		'
7479               	; 		' THE FIRST FEW PASSES ARE THE STEP ON. Walking on, his feet are on
7480               	; 		' the floor and the bottom tread is 4 to 7 px above them, so he
7481               	; 		' climbs at 2 px a pass until he catches it (the tread is rising at
7482               	; 		' 1, so the gap closes at 1 a pass) and then rides with it. Jumping
7483               	; 		' on he lands ON a tread, so eson is 0 and this never runs.

8948               	;
8949               	; 	' THE VICTROLA, AS CHARACTERS. It never moves, so a sprite spent a
8950               	; 	' scan-line slot on something that can be painted once when the screen is
8951               	; 	' drawn -- and at one 16x16 sprite it could only ever be one colour and
8952               	; 	' one size. Four cells is twice the area for no sprite at all.
8953               	; 	'
8954               	; 	' It stands ON the slab, so it fills the band's rows 2 and 3; row 4 is
8955               	; 	' the floor bar itself -- and a PRIZE uses those same two rows.
8956               	; 	'
8957               	; 	' THEY CAN SHARE A BAND, AND THE CLAIM THAT USED TO BE HERE WAS WRONG.
8958               	; 	' It said the two never share a screen because "genstore keeps prizes off
8959               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards". That stopped being true the moment
8960               	; 	' hazard placement moved into the per-Krook stor_lvl table, and nothing
8961               	; 	' noticed, because the prize table is not part of the level table and
8962               	; 	' every check was written about one object at a time. Two money bags ended
8963               	; 	' up standing on a radio -- not fighting it, since the two routines poke
8964               	; 	' different cells and the later writer simply wins, so they read as one
8965               	; 	' merged object.
8966               	; 	'
8967               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS THEM APART IS COLUMNS. A radio stands at column 7, 15 or 23
8968               	; 	' (see lrc below); genstore's _off_the_rack nudges a prize clear of all
8969               	; 	' three, and checklevels.py reads that arithmetic back out of THIS file
8970               	; 	' and fails the build on any overlap.
8971               	; 	'
8972               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
8973               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
8974               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
8975               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
8976               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
8977               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
8978               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
8979               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
8980               	; 	'
8981               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the
8982               	; 	' top shopping floor is the ROOF DECK, a different character altogether,
8983               	; 	' and writing a floor bar over it would punch a hole in the roof.
8984               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
8985               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
8986               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because
8987               	; 	' a counter reads as one object. The whole unit goes: walk outward along
8988               	; 	' the band's row 2 while the cell is still a shelf top, clearing it and
8989               	; 	' its bottom half together.
8990               	; 	'
8991               	; 	' Bounded at eight steps. The runs are five, so eight is slack rather
8992               	; 	' than a guess -- and an unbounded walk would run off the end of the row
8993               	; 	' if the name table ever held something unexpected.
8994               	; 	#if NES
8995               	; 	' WHAT THE TEMPLATE PUT IN THIS CELL, for a target that cannot read its
8996               	; 	' own video memory back. #nta is the offset INSIDE the band (0-159) and
8997               	; 	' nbl is the band; the answer is the byte SCREEN blitted there.
8998               	; 	'
8999               	; 	' This is the same arithmetic the blit itself does in draw_band --
9000               	; 	' template id out of stor_ix for (band, screen), times 160, plus the
9001               	; 	' offset -- so the two cannot disagree about what is on screen. It is
9002               	; 	' reading what the cell MEANS, not guessing from where the cell is: a
9003               	; 	' coordinate is a fact about this layout, the character is a fact about
9004               	; 	' the world, and only the second is safe to erase on.
9005               	; 	' SIXTEEN PATTERNS INTO THE BORROWED SLOTS, ONE VBLANK EACH.
9006               	; 	'
9007               	; 	' This is what esc_stand and esc_run cost on this machine. Four sprites is
9008               	; 	' 16 patterns and **a tile here is SIXTEEN bytes** -- two bitplanes -- so
9009               	; 	' the swap is 256 bytes. Three ways to spend that, and only one works:
9010               	; 	'
9011               	; 	'   nes_def         rendering off, ~2 frames of DARK SCREEN every mount.
9012               	; 	'                   This is the flash that was reported for three sessions.
9013               	; 	'   resident art    no upload at all -- but it needs 16 free patterns per
9014               	; 	'                   facing and there are only twelve free in the whole
9015               	; 	'                   table. Tried, and it overwrote Harry's left-facing legs.
9016               	; 	'   queued, chunked <- this. 64 bytes a vblank, four vblanks, picture up
9017               	; 	'                   the whole time.
9018               	; 	'
9019               	; 	' FOUR CHUNKS BECAUSE ONE WILL NOT FIT. The NMI's copy loop runs to the end
9020               	; 	' of its descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and the PPUADDR/PPUSCROLL
9021               	; 	' restore that follows it re-points the PPU mid-frame if it runs late --
9022               	; 	' which is the whole picture jumping for a frame. About 1679 cycles are
9023               	; 	' available after OAM DMA and a copy costs 50 + 14 a byte, so 64 bytes
9024               	; 	' (946) is comfortable and 256 (3634) is not. The WAITs are load-bearing:
9025               	; 	' PPUBUF accumulates for a whole pass, so without them all four descriptors
9026               	; 	' would flush in one vblank and cost exactly what the single call did.
9027               	; 	' checkvblank.py sums the descriptors BETWEEN WAITs for this reason.
9028               	; 	'
9029               	; 	' The cost is four frames at a mount or a dismount, once each, against two
9030               	; 	' frames of black. The caller sets #nsrc; nes_chrinit copies nchr, ncnt,
9031               	; 	' #ncol and nink into zero page rather than consuming the variables, so
9032               	; 	' they only need setting once.
9033               	; 	'
9034               	; 	' THE INTERMEDIATE STATE IS VISIBLE and that is accepted: for a frame or
9035               	; 	' two Harry is part standing and part running. He is stepping onto a
9036               	; 	' staircase at the time, which is exactly when a limb changing shape reads
9037               	; 	' as him changing pose.
9038               	; nes_swp16:
9039               	; 	' HARRY COMES OFF THE SCREEN FIRST, because this takes four frames.
9040               	; 	'
9041               	; 	' The swap is 256 bytes and a vblank carries about a hundred, so it goes as
9042               	; 	' four queued chunks with a WAIT between them (see below). The game loop is
9043               	; 	' stopped for those frames but the PPU is not, so whatever is half-written
9044               	; 	' is on screen: for a frame or two Harry was part standing and part
9045               	; 	' running -- reported as a glitch when he steps off a flight, and it is
9046               	; 	' one. All four of his sprites differ between the two poses, so there is no
9047               	; 	' ordering of the chunks that stays coherent.
9048               	; 	'
9049               	; 	' He is hidden instead. Four frames of absence at the exact moment he steps
9050               	; 	' on or off a staircase reads as nothing at all, where a figure assembled
9051               	; 	' out of two poses reads as a fault. draw_actors puts him back on its next
9052               	; 	' pass -- no flag to clear, because it writes all four slots every time.
9053               	; 	'
9054               	; 	' AND THE OAM MIRRORS WITH HIM. nes_oam2 copies slots 0-27 into 28-55 to
9055               	; 	' make each 16x16 actor two NES sprites, and it only runs at the end of
9056               	; 	' draw_actors -- which is not running during these WAITs. Without the call
9057               	; 	' below his left half would vanish and his RIGHT half would stay, which is
9058               	; 	' a worse artefact than the one being fixed.
9059               	; 	SPRITE 4,SPRHID,0,0,0
9060               	; 	SPRITE 5,SPRHID,0,0,0
9061               	; 	SPRITE 6,SPRHID,0,0,0
9062               	; 	SPRITE 7,SPRHID,0,0,0
9063               	; 	ASM JSR nes_oam2
9064               	; 	ASM JSR nes_suitcases
9065               	; 	nchr = P_HSTB

9091               	; nes_def:
9092               	; 	' WHAT DEFINE WOULD HAVE DONE. CVBasic implements no DEFINE at all for the
9093               	; 	' NES, on the reading that patterns live in cartridge CHR ROM -- but an
9094               	; 	' iNES header with a CHR-bank count of ZERO asks for 8 KB of CHR-RAM
9095               	; 	' instead, and that is the header CVBasic emits whenever the program uses
9096               	; 	' no BITMAP/CHRROM statement. So the pattern table here is ordinary VRAM
9097               	; 	' and this is the write. assets/nes_chr.asm carries the routine and the
9098               	; 	' reasoning; the caller sets #nsrc, nchr, ncnt and ntab.
9099               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrup
9100               	; 	RETURN
9101               	;
9102               	; 	' AND THE SAME THING WITHOUT LOSING A FRAME. nes_def turns rendering off
9103               	; 	' and waits for a vblank the NMI therefore never services, so the game's
9104               	; 	' own WAIT then waits for the one after -- about two frames a call. That
9105               	; 	' is free at setup and ruinous anywhere that runs repeatedly. It builds
9106               	; 	' the same bytes into `nesb` and hands the NMI a single copy descriptor
9107               	; 	' instead. See assets/nes_chr.asm.
9108               	; 	'
9109               	; 	' THE NAME IS HISTORICAL: it was written for esc_tick, which redefines six
9110               	; 	' characters EVERY PASS on the two escalator screens and ran visibly slow
9111               	; 	' on nes_def. Nothing about it is escalator-specific -- it takes the same
9112               	; 	' inputs as nes_def plus #nesb, and the title's marquee uses it too, where
9113               	; 	' nes_def was switching the picture off twice a step and reading as a
9114               	; 	' flashing title screen.
9115               	; 	'
9116               	; 	' #nesb must point at a buffer of at least ncnt*16 bytes and is set once
9117               	; 	' in init_tables, which runs before boot: and therefore before the title.
9118               	; nes_escd:
9119               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrq
9120               	; 	RETURN

9214               	;
9215               	; 	' A PILLAR'S CAP MAY BE CLEARED; AN END WALL'S MAY NOT. beam_one stamps
9216               	; 	' both into the slab row of the band above, but they mean different
9217               	; 	' things. SLABP is the top of a free-standing pillar: a radio or a prize
9218               	; 	' stands in front of the pillar, so leaving its cap up there hangs a grey
9219               	; 	' stub over the fixture and that is what this routine exists to remove.
9220               	; 	' SLABE and ROOFSE are written ONLY at column 0 and column 31 -- read
9221               	; 	' beam_one, they are the two edge cases -- and there they are the
9222               	; 	' BUILDING'S OUTSIDE WALL, carrying its brick bond up through the floor
9223               	; 	' above. Clearing those took the support out from under the storey above
9224               	; 	' at the very edge of the screen, so the second floor visibly rested on
9225               	; 	' nothing.
9226               	; 	'
9227               	; 	' It could only ever show on the ESCALATOR screens, which is exactly how
9228               	; 	' it was reported -- one side, then mirrored on the other. The flight
9229               	; 	' fills the middle of an escalator band, so that screen's radio or prize
9230               	; 	' is pushed right out against the end wall; on every other screen no
9231               	; 	' fixture sits close enough for the two-cell clear at #bca and #bca+1 to
9232               	; 	' reach column 0 or 31.
9233               	; beam_clear:
9234               cvb_BEAM_CLEAR
9235               	; 	' A BEAM TOP IS NOT IN THE TEMPLATE. beam_one VPOKEs it into the row
9236               	; 	' ABOVE each band, out of the pillar-column table -- so on the NES this
9237               	; 	' asks that same table rather than the PPU, and #bca sits one row above
9238               	; 	' the band, which is why it cannot go through nes_tpl.
9239               	; 	'
9240               	; 	' IT ALSO REPRODUCES beam_one'S EXCLUSION OF COLUMNS 0 AND 31. Those
9241               	; 	' carry SLABE/ROOFSE, the building's OUTSIDE WALL, not a pillar cap --
9242               	; 	' and clearing structure because an erase routine could not tell the

9929               	; 	' the bounce advanced once per PASS -- so whether a jump cleared a ball
9930               	; 	' depended on how busy the screen was, and the frame-by-frame property
9931               	; 	' checkball.py proves was exact only at fdv = 1.

9934               	; 	' game: a 32-phase arc would drop from about 1.35 s to 0.55 s, balls
9935               	; 	' bouncing 2.4x faster everywhere. So it gets a fraction of its own --
9936               	; 	' 25/64 of a phase per frame is 23.4 phases a second, against the 23.8 it

10204               	; 	' ONE STEP OF A FRACTIONAL SPEED, FOR WHOEVER IS MOVING.
10205               	; 	'
10206               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
10207               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
10208               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
10209               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
10210               	; 	'
10211               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
10212               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
10213               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
10214               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10215               	; 	'
10216               	; 	' Three drains support up to 192/64 units per frame. The remainder
10217               	; 	' is below 64, so the byte addition cannot exceed 255. Planes use
10218               	; 	' two-pixel units and double the result outside this shared routine.
10219               	; 	' Other actors retain pixel units and their existing movement rates.
10220               	; 	'
10221               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
10222               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
10223               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
10224               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
10225               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
10226               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.

10334               	; 	' wrong way.

10732               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
10733               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
10734               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
10735               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
10736               	; 	' runs every pass.
10737               	; 	'
10738               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
10739               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
10740               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
10741               	; 	'
10742               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
10743               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
10744               	; 	'
10745               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
10746               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
10747               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
10748               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
10749               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
10750               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
10751               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short
10752               	; 	' of his own escape. checkchase.py now counts these IFs and refuses a
10753               	; 	' speed the drains cannot deliver.
10754               	; 	'
10755               	; 	' 7, NOT 6, AND THE REASON IS MEASURED. Tracked off the reference video
10756               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 4a), the 2600's Kelly covers 0.40 screen widths a second and
10757               	; 	' its Harry 0.193 -- a ratio of 2.07. At hsp4 = 6 ours was 2.67, and the
10758               	; 	' crook visibly strolled. 7 brings it to 2.29. 8 would match the original
10759               	; 	' exactly and cannot be used: Kelly's route here is 1.95x Harry's, so a
10760               	; 	' speed ratio of 2.0 leaves the on-foot chase 0.2 s of slack, which is no

10863               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
10864               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
10865               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
10866               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
10867               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
10868               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
10869               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
10870               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10871               	; 	'
10872               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
10873               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
10874               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
10875               	; 	'
10876               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
10877               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
10878               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
10879               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
10880               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
10881               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
10882               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
10883               	; 	'
10884               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
10885               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
10886               	; 	'
10887               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
10888               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
10889               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
10890               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
10891               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
10892               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
10893               	; 	'
10894               	; 	' The clamp and the drains live in pace_step now, with the reasoning; the
10895               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen
10896               	; 	' against TIME 04 on a light one when the clamp was 3, and 00 against 09
10897               	; 	' before any of this.
10898               	; 	'
10899               	; 	' The ESCALATOR RIDE is deliberately untouched: it returns above this,
10900               	; 	' clocked one step per pass to stay locked to the moving staircase. A rider
10901               	; 	' advanced by the frame delta either drifts off the treads or makes the
10902               	; 	' steps run backwards (CLAUDE.md 3A, DESIGN.md 0f). It is about 3% of his
10903               	; 	' journey.
10904               	; 	'
10905               	; 	' `hanim` still advances by hspd and is still an ODOMETER -- pixels
10906               	; 	' travelled, not time -- so the run cycle stays locked to the ground at any
10907               	; 	' rate. A 9 px step moves it exactly one pose of its 8 px beat.

11368               	;
11369               	; 	' ======================================================================
11370               	; 	' COLLISIONS -- pure arithmetic against RAM, no VDP reads
11371               	; 	' ======================================================================
11372               	; 	' Kelly's box is [kfh, kfh + kh) above the slab; an obstacle's is
11373               	; 	' [ohb, oht). The ball's inset hitbox is what makes 8..10 avoidable both
11374               	; 	' ways -- without it there is a height at which the ball can be neither
11375               	; 	' jumped nor ducked, and an unavoidable hazard is not difficulty.
11376               	; 	' ONE HIT PER CONTACT, WITH A REFRACTORY PERIOD.
11377               	; 	'
11378               	; 	' The overlap test is true on every frame the player is touching
11379               	; 	' something, so with no latch at all one clumsy cart charges nine seconds
11380               	; 	' several times over -- and what the player sees is the clock jumping by
11381               	; 	' 27, from which the only available conclusion is that the penalty is
11382               	; 	' broken.
11383               	; 	'
11384               	; 	' A latch that clears on the first non-overlapping frame is still not
11385               	; 	' enough, and the case that breaks it is the BOUNCING BALL: it rises off
11386               	; 	' the player between bounces, which is a genuine loss of contact, so a
11387               	; 	' player standing still under one is taxed on every single bounce while
11388               	; 	' being given no opportunity to do anything about it. Technically two
11389               	; 	' collisions; in play, one situation.
11390               	; 	'
11391               	; 	' So obht() is a countdown, not a flag. A hit sets it to HITREF; it ticks
11392               	; 	' down only while the player is CLEAR, and the same obstacle cannot charge
11393               	; 	' again until it reaches zero. Contact holds the count up, so parking
11394               	; 	' inside something never earns a second penalty either.
11395               	; coll_obst:
11396               cvb_COLL_OBST

11870               	; 	' THE FLOOR CLEARS WHEN YOU ARE HIT, and stays clear until you re-enter
11871               	; 	' the screen. Nine seconds is a heavy penalty on a fifty-unit clock, and
11872               	; 	' taking it while still standing among the things that charged it -- with
11873               	; 	' a second hazard 48 px behind the first -- is how one mistake becomes
11874               	; 	' three. Clearing the row makes the penalty a single event you can walk
11875               	; 	' away from.
11876               	; 	'

12182               	; draw_actors:
12183               cvb_DRAW_ACTORS
12184               	; 	' RIDING WITH THE DOORS SHUT: HIDE HIM AND DO NOT DRAW HIM AT ALL.
12185               	; 	'
12186               	; 	' This test used to sit AFTER his sprites had been written, so every pass
12187               	; 	' placed him at his old floor and then hid him again. That is not free.
12188               	; 	' CVBasic's SPRITE writes a RAM mirror which the vblank ISR copies to
12189               	; 	' VRAM, so a vblank landing BETWEEN the draw and the hide latches the
12190               	; 	' visible state for a frame -- and draw_actors is long (Kelly, Harry,
12191               	; 	' eight obstacles) while a pass on the lift screen spans two or three
12192               	; 	' frames, so it happened constantly. He flickered at the floor he had
12193               	; 	' just left, which reads as a drawing bug rather than as a journey.
12194               	; 	'
12195               	; 	' Deciding BEFORE drawing costs one test and cannot race the ISR at all:
12196               	; 	' the mirror never holds a position to be caught with.
12197               	; 	IF klst = ST_ELEV THEN
12198 DF2A D020  34 	movb @cvb_KLST,r0
     DF2C 21BA

12644               	; 	' HIS ARMS SWING, on the same bit of the animation counter that picks the
12645               	; 	' legs -- so the arm that is forward is the one opposite the leading leg,

12650               	; 	' arm swing keyed to bit 8 completed twice for every one pass of the legs:
12651               	; 	' the top half of him flapping at double the speed of the bottom half.
12652               	; 	' That is the jig. It is not a drawing problem and no amount of redrawing
12653               	; 	' the legs would have touched it.

12656               	; 	' also the right PHASE: beat 1 leads with one leg and beat 3 with the

12772               	; 	' legs under a motionless torso reads as a dance rather than as travel.
12773               	; 	'

12775               	; 	' keep their y, so the planted foot stays on the floor and the figure
12776               	; 	' stretches at the waist instead of hopping. Lifting the legs too would be
12777               	; 	' a jump.

12780               	; 	' cycle's LOW beat bit. IT MUST MOVE WITH THE BEAT BITS ABOVE IT: on the
12781               	; 	' wrong bit he rises and falls twice per stride, a second clock inside one
12782               	; 	' figure, which is the flapping of DESIGN.md 0j2 in the vertical.

13305               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
13306               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
13307               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
13308               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
13309               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
13310               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
13311               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
13312               	; 	'
13313               	; 	' So the ANIMATION is the clock here, and the rider is paced from it --
13314               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
13315               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
13316               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
13317               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
13318               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
13319               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.

13333               	; 	#if NES
13334               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
13335               	; 	'
13336               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
13337               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
13338               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
13339               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
13340               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
13341               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
13342               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
13343               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
13344               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
13345               	; 	'
13346               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
13347               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
13348               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
13349               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
13350               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
13351               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
13352               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
13353               	; 	'
13354               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
13355               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
13356               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
13357               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
13358               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
13359               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
13360               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
13361               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
13362               	; 	' with room to spare.
13363               	; 	'
13364               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
13365               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
13366               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
13367               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
13368               	; 	WAIT
13369               	; 	#endif
13370               	; 	' ONLY THE CELLS THAT MOVE, AND ONLY THIS SCREEN'S. genart.py measures
13371               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them
13372               	; 	' that cross a floor -- and groups them WEST then EAST, because only one
13373               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
13374               	; 	' 7 an east one.
13375               	; 	'
13376               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
13377               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
13378               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
13379               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.
13380               	; 	'
13381               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO

14009               	;
14010               	; 	' fbase = the top pixel row of level fl's FOUR px band, without a
14011               	; 	' multiply. Four levels at four rows is 16 of the canvas's 24 pixel
14012               	; 	' rows, and the other eight are deliberately empty -- four above and
14013               	; 	' four below -- so the instrument sits in the black with air around it
14014               	; 	' instead of butting against the shop floor above and the screen edge
14015               	; 	' below. The +4 is that top margin.
14016               	; scan_base:
14017               cvb_SCAN_BASE
14018               	; 	' A LEVEL BAND IS SIX PIXEL ROWS ON THE NES AND FOUR ON THE TI.
14019               	; 	'
14020               	; 	' It was six everywhere once. It shrank to four to buy eight empty pixel
14021               	; 	' rows -- four above the instrument and four below -- so the scanner did
14022               	; 	' not butt against the shop floor above it and the bottom of the screen.
14023               	; 	'
14024               	; 	' On the NES that margin now comes from somewhere else: the name table is
14025               	; 	' thirty rows to the TI's twenty-four, so the strip runs past the canvas to
14026               	; 	' the bottom edge and the grey either side of the instrument is real cells
14027               	; 	' rather than blank rows inside it. That gives the band its two rows back,
14028               	; 	' and the instrument goes from 16 pixels tall to 24 -- half again, which is
14029               	; 	' what "not quite so vertically thin" asks for.
14030               	; 	'
14031               	; 	' The TI cannot follow: its name table ENDS at row 23, the scanner is on
14032               	; 	' the last three rows, and there is nowhere to put the margin. So the band
14033               	; 	' height is per-target and every row offset below is derived from it.
14034               	; 	'
14035               	; 	' An IF ladder rather than arithmetic: four levels, and x6 needs a temp
14036               	; 	' this program has no RAM for (two bytes free).

14192               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
14193               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a
14194               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
14195               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
14196               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
14197               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).

14200               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
14201               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
14202               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
14203               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
14204               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
14205               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
14206               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
14207               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
14208               	; 	'
14209               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
14210               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
14211               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
14212               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
14213               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
14214               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick
14215               	; 	' carried up through the bar above them. ENDWALL appears only on
14216               	; 	' screens 0 and 7, which is exactly why it was reported as happening

14862               	; #if NES
14863               	; 	' ----------------------------------------------------------------------
14864               	; 	' Attributes select a palette per 16x16 quadrant. gennescolor.py derives
14865               	; 	' eight screen tables; draw_screen stages one in nesb, masks fixtures,
14866               	; 	' then uploads all 64 bytes through nes_attrs_put within one vblank.
14867               	; 	' A MESSAGE BOX GOES GOLD ON DARK BLUE, and the caller says which four
14868               	; 	' bytes in #nav.
14869               	; 	'
14870               	; 	' The text's paper is index 1 and its ink index 3 (see the font upload);
14871               	; 	' over the store those are P0's green and gold -- the same green the box is
14872               	; 	' sitting on, which is what made the messages hard to read. P1 is the HUD's
14873               	; 	' palette, dark blue and gold, so pointing the box's attribute bytes at it
14874               	; 	' gives a message the same treatment as the score line.
14875               	; 	'
14876               	; 	' FOUR BYTES AND NOT ONE MORE. An attribute byte covers four characters by
14877               	; 	' four, and the box is sized and placed to cover exactly four of them
14878               	; 	' (gentitle.py BOX_ROW/BOX_COL/BOX_W): byte columns 2..5, which is name
14879               	; 	' columns 8..23. Anything wider would recolour shop floor beside the box.
14880               	; 	'
14881               	; 	' THIS IS A ROUTINE BECAUSE IT WAS WRITTEN OUT TWICE AND MISSED A THIRD
14882               	; 	' TIME. GOT HIM! kept the store's colours while the other boxes changed,
14883               	; 	' and nothing failed -- it is a readable message in the wrong palette.
14884               	; 	' checkmsg.py now fails the build if a message box is drawn without one of
14885               	; 	' these beside it.
14886               	; 	'
14887               	; 	' Nothing puts them back, because nothing needs to: every path out of a
14888               	; 	' message box redraws the screen, and draw_screen calls nes_attr, which
14889               	; 	' rewrites all sixty-four.
14890               	; nes_boxatt:
14891               	; 	WAIT
14892               	; 	IF #nav = 9178 THEN
14893               	; 		' GAME OVER begins in the lower half of one attribute row.
14894               	; 		' Preserve the surrounding halves from the actual screen upload.
14895               	; 		FOR nai = 0 TO 3
14896               	; 			nink = (nmsg(nai) AND 15) OR 80
14897               	; 			VPOKE #nav,nink
14898               	; 			#nsrc = #nav + 8
14899               	; 			nink = (nmsg(nai) AND 240) OR 15
14900               	; 			VPOKE #nsrc,nink
14901               	; 			#nav = #nav + 1

14904               	; 	ELSE

14908               	; 			#nav = #nav + 1
14909               	; 		NEXT nai

14911               	; 	END IF

14918               	;
14919               	; nes_attr:

15402               	;
15403               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
15404               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
15405               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
15406               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
15407               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
15408               	; 	'
15409               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
15410               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
15411               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
15412               	; 	'
15413               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
15414               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
15415               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
15416               	; 	'
15417               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
15418               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
15419               	; 	'
15420               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
15421               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
15422               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
15423               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
15424               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
15425               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
15426               	; 	'
15427               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
15428               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
15429               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
15430               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
15431               	; 	'
15432               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
15433               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
15434               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
15435               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)
15436               	; bonus_count:
15437               cvb_BONUS_COUNT

15492               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS TALLY B -- a blip that COUNTS rather than a buzz that
15493               	; 	' ratchets. Two frames on and two off at 1,036 Hz (divisor 108), against
15494               	; 	' the 373 Hz it was: the pitch is what separates a count from the
15495               	; 	' timer's own low tick, and the shorter gap makes ten of them a run
15496               	; 	' rather than a queue.
15497               	; 	'
15498               	; 	' NES uses a lower 415 Hz pulse tick (divisor 270); the full catch path
15499               	; 	' in iNES was silent at divisor 108. snd_off has freed channel 1.
15500               	; 	' Other targets keep channel 2. The effect table uses it for the upper voice of a
15501               	; 	' two-note effect, so a tick here cannot cancel a sustained tone on
15502               	; 	' channel 1 (CLAUDE.md 3A: two SOUNDs on one channel back to back just
15503               	; 	' cancel the first). The bench plays B on channel 0 because the bench
15504               	; 	' has nothing else running.
15505               	; 	#if NES
15506               	; 	' iNES needs control/volume before the pitch write to start a note.
15507               	; 	IF spt = 0 THEN
15508               	; 		SOUND 1,,12
15509               	; 		SOUND 1,270

15579               	;
15580               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
15581               	; 	'
15582               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
15583               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
15584               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
15585               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
15586               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
15587               	; 	'
15588               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
15589               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
15590               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
15591               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
15592               	; 	' counting stops.
15593               	;
15594               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
15595               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
15596               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
15597               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
15598               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
15599               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
15600               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
15601               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
15602               	; 	'
15603               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
15604               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
15605               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).

15824               	; 	' Silence every channel FIRST. SOUND latches, and the per-channel decay
15825               	; 	' counters are not ticked inside this loop -- a tone still sounding when

15827               	; 	' CVBasic sticky-audio failure.

15829               	; 	' ticked by the main loop, so anything still sounding when the loop stops

15831               	; 	' whatever replaced the loop takes. That is where the long beep over the
15832               	; 	' bonus tally came from: not the tally's own note, which turns itself off

15840               	; 	' NOISE channel. So a step ringing when Harry was caught was never turned
15841               	; 	' off: it hissed through the whole bonus tally and did not stop until the

15954               	;
15955               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
15956               	; 	'
15957               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
15958               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
15959               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
15960               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
15961               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
15962               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
15963               	; 	'
15964               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
15965               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
15966               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
15967               	; 	'
15968               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
15969               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
15970               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
15971               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
15972               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
15973               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
15974               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
15975               	; 	'
15976               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
15977               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
15978               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
15979               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
15980               	; 	'
15981               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
15982               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
15983               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
15984               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
15985               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
15986               	; 	'
15987               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
15988               	; 	' did not finish.
15989               	; pause_beat:
15990               cvb_PAUSE_BEAT

15997               	; 	' call sites would have cost code to say the same thing worse.
15998               	; 	'
15999               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNT AND NOT THE WAITS. sfx_tick runs once per pass, so it

16421               	;
16422               	; 	' THE LOW-TIME WARNING IS SILENT. There was a beep a second under ten, and
16423               	; 	' it was the wrong instrument for the job: the last ten seconds are the
16424               	; 	' busiest part of a round, so a repeating tone arrives exactly when the
16425               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
16426               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
16427               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
16428               	;
16429               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
16430               	; 	'
16431               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
16432               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
16433               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
16434               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
16435               	; 	'
16436               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
16437               	; 	'
16438               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
16439               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
16440               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
16441               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
16442               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
16443               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
16444               	; 	'
16445               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
16446               	; 	'
16447               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
16448               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
16449               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
16450               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
16451               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
16452               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
16453               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
16454               	; 	'
16455               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
16456               	; 	'
16457               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
16458               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
16459               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
16460               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
16461               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
16462               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
16463               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
16464               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
16465               	; 	'
16466               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
16467               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
16468               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
16469               	; 	'
16470               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
16471               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
16472               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
16473               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
16474               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
16475               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
16476               	; 	'
16477               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
16478               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
16479               	; 	'
16480               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
16481               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
16482               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
16483               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
16484               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer
16485               	; 	' gets, and the reason the bench and the game cannot sound identical.
16486               	; 	'
16487               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.
16488               	; 	'
16489               	; 	' VOLUME 9, WHICH IS UNDER EVERYTHING ELSE ON PURPOSE. The hit, the prize
16490               	; 	' and the jump are 12 and 13, and they happen ONCE; footsteps play for the
16491               	; 	' whole round. At 13 they were level with the events they are supposed to
16492               	; 	' sit beneath, so the effects that carry information had nothing to stand
16493               	; 	' out from. The tone version was 7 for the same reason -- noise does read

16820               	;
16821               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
16822               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
16823               	; 	'
16824               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
16825               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
16826               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
16827               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
16828               	; 	'
16829               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
16830               	; 	'
16831               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
16832               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
16833               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
16834               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
16835               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
16836               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
16837               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
16838               	; 	'
16839               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
16840               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
16841               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
16842               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
16843               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
16844               	; 	'
16845               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
16846               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
16847               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
16848               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
16849               	; 	#if TI994A
16850               	; 	BANK 2
16851      0778     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$
     **** ****     > .rept

17400               	;
17401               	; 	' THE COLOUR TABLE, 472 bytes of the same value ($B4 = light yellow ink on dark blue).
17402               	; 	'
17403               	; 	' Loaded with DEFINE COLOR 32,59,font_col, which is ONE synchronous call that
17404               	; 	' writes all three screen thirds (define_color always does the LDIRVM3 triple
17405               	; 	' copy). It replaced a VPOKE loop that wrote this one value 1,416 times paced by
17406               	; 	' 24 WAITs -- the largest scripted delay in the boot, and the reason the title
17407               	; 	' screen used to fill in visibly rather than appearing at once.
17408               	; 	'
17409               	; 	' EIGHT BYTES PER CHARACTER, not one. Supply fewer and DEFINE COLOR reads
17410               	; 	' whatever follows in ROM as colour data, with no error at build or run time.
17411               	;
17412               	; #if NES
17413               	; 	' NES uses nes_fcol; omit this identical 472-byte TMS colour table.
17414               	; #else
17415               	; font_col:
17416               cvb_FONT_COL

18148               	; 	INCLUDE "art.bas"
18149               	; 	' Keystone Kapers art -- GENERATED by assets/genart.py. Do not edit; regenerate.
18150               	; 	'
18151               	; 	' EVERY SPRITE IS 16x16: sprite size and magnification are GLOBAL on the
18152               	; 	' TMS9918, so small objects are drawn small INSIDE a 16x16 box rather than
18153               	; 	' being small sprites.
18154               	; 	'
18155               	; 	' EVERY 8-PX OBJECT SITS IN ROWS 8-15 OF ITS BOX, ducked Kelly included, so
18156               	; 	' one rule places them all: bottom edge = y + 16, and a thing resting on the
18157               	; 	' floor is at y = FLOORY - 16.
18158               	; 	'
18159               	; 	' Sprite bytes are QUADRANT-ORDERED: 16 rows of the left half, then 16 of
18160               	; 	' the right. Every block is an EVEN number of bytes -- an odd DATA BYTE run
18161               	; 	' silently misaligns every word table after it (CLAUDE.md 3A).
18162               	;
18163               	; spr_kelly:	' Kelly: RIGHT hat/face/two merged run bodies/two FREE slots/duck hat/face/body, then the same LEFT (+36). The run bodies carry tunic AND legs, so a frame is one sprite, and standing is run frame 1. Patterns 0..68

19395               	; 	INCLUDE "store.bas"
19396               	; 	' Keystone Kapers store -- GENERATED by assets/genstore.py. Do not edit.
19397               	; 	'
19398               	; 	' EIGHT band templates of 5 rows x 32 cols (160 bytes each) plus a 32-byte
19399               	; 	' index over (level, screen). The whole 8-screen, 4-level building is about
19400               	; 	' 1.3 KB instead of the 5,120 bytes it would cost to store literally.
19401               	; 	'
19402               	; 	' All eight templates are ONE contiguous block under ONE label, so a band
19403               	; 	' blit is
19404               	; 	'     SCREEN stor_tpl, tpl*160, toprow*32, 32, 5, 32
19405               	; 	' with no label ladder -- SCREEN needs a literal label and a label cannot be
19406               	; 	' chosen by a variable, which is why RallyX needed a 4-way IF over its maze
19407               	; 	' tables. One block sidesteps it.
19408               	; 	'
19409               	; 	' 160 is EVEN, so this cannot leave the location counter odd and misalign
19410               	; 	' the word tables defined after it.
19411               	; 	'
19412               	; 	' template ids:
19413               	; 	'   0 T_AISLE_A
19414               	; 	'   1 T_AISLE_B
19415               	; 	'   2 T_ESC_W
19416               	; 	'   3 T_ESC_E
19417               	; 	'   4 T_ELEV
19418               	; 	'   5 T_ROOF0
19419               	; 	'   6 T_ROOF1
19420               	; 	'   7 T_ROOF2
19421               	; 	'   8 T_ROOF3
19422               	; 	'   9 T_ROOF4
19423               	; 	'   10 T_ROOF5
19424               	; 	'   11 T_ROOF6
19425               	; 	'   12 T_ROOF7
19426               	; 	'   13 T_END_W
19427               	; 	'   14 T_END_E
19428               	;
19429               	; stor_tpl:	' 15 templates x 160 bytes
19430               cvb_STOR_TPL
19431               	; 	DATA BYTE 154,154,154,154,107,154,154,154,154,154,154,107,154,154,154,154

20046               	; 	' THE SKYLINE'S LAST BAND WITHOUT ITS YELLOW, high nibble ink, low nibble
20047               	; 	' paper, one byte a scan line -- the same shape genart emits into
20048               	; 	' store_col. SKY2 is white-on-9 throughout instead of turning to paper 10
20049               	; 	' at row 4; BLDGL holds its blue one row longer and then meets its own
20050               	; 	' grey wall. Both are the generated bytes with 10 replaced by 9 and
20051               	; 	' nothing else changed. See setup_rest.
20052               	; #if NES
20053               	; nes_sky2c:
20054               	; 	DATA BYTE $F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9
20055               	; nes_bldlc:
20056               	; 	DATA BYTE $B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$BE,$BE,$BE
20057               	; #endif
20058               	;
20059               	; 	' THE IN-GAME FONT'S COLOUR, one byte a scan line and eight a character for
20060               	; 	' all 59 of them. $B4 is light yellow on dark blue -- ink index 3, paper index 1 --
20061               	; 	' and which colours those are is then the attribute table's business, per
20062               	; 	' region: dark blue behind the HUD, the store's green behind a message box.
20063               	; 	'
20064               	; 	' 472 bytes of one repeated value. That reads like waste and is the cheap
20065               	; 	' option: ROM is three budgets here and this is not the scarce one, while
20066               	; 	' the alternative is a second font (impossible -- only eleven free codes)
20067               	; 	' or a new uploader parameter (no RAM -- two bytes left).
